name: Dollar-cost averaging (baseline)

origin.source_title: Cost averaging: Invest now or temporarily hold your cash?

how_it_works.simple: Instead of investing all your money at once, you put in the same amount every month. You buy more when prices are low and less when they are high.
how_it_works.analogy: Like filling your car with the same 40 dollars of gas every week no matter the price per gallon.
how_it_works.precise: Split a lump sum into equal tranches invested at fixed intervals. Because markets drift upward on average, holding cash while waiting lowers expected return; DCA mainly reduces regret and timing risk rather than raising returns.

rule: Invest 1/k of the available cash into the target asset (for example an S&P 500 ETF or BTC) on the first trading day of each month for k months, holding the rest in cash; compare against investing everything on day one.
data_needed: Monthly total-return index of the target asset
economic_rationale: No return edge is claimed; Vanguard frames it as a behavioral tool that lowers the chance of investing everything just before a fall.
why_it_might_fail: Vanguard finds lump sum beat cost averaging 61.6 to 73.7 percent of the time across markets from 1976 to 2022, because the uninvested cash misses the equity premium.

reported_results.source: Vanguard Research, Finlay and Zorn (2023), summarized on Vanguard NL page
reported_results.market: US, UK, Canada, Europe, Australia, EM, global equity and balanced portfolios
reported_results.notes: Lump sum won 61.6 to 73.7 percent of the time; 1-year outcomes were 2.2 percent higher for 100 percent equity, 1.8 percent for 60/40, 1.2 percent for 40/60 when invested at once. Base case splits into three monthly tranches.

relevance.reason: A simple, honest benchmark for parity: any FX strategy should be compared with both lump-sum and DCA into the S&P 500.
